props.title: Crash and Burn

sections.content: **Crash and Burn** (2016) tells the fascinating story of Tommy Byrne, often called "the greatest Formula 1 driver you've never heard of." This documentary follows a similar path to Senna (2010), but focuses on racing's dark underbelly rather than its champions. Like Rush (2013), it captures the raw intensity of 1980s motorsport, but through the lens of a working-class Irish driver who had the talent but lacked the political connections and financial backing to succeed in F1's elite world.

sections.content: The film fits into a broader tradition of motorsport documentaries that expose the sport's class divisions. 1: Life on the Limit (2013) similarly explores F1's dangerous past and the socioeconomic barriers faced by drivers. Williams (2017) examines how even successful teams struggled with the sport's financial demands. These films reveal how raw talent often takes a backseat to commercial interests in professional racing.

Byrne's story particularly resonates with other documentaries about "almost-made-it" athletes like **Next Goal Wins** (2014) and **The Other Dream Team** (2012). His brash personality and undeniable skill make him a compelling subject, while his ultimate failure to break through reflects broader issues in professional sports, similar to themes explored in **The Price of Gold** (2014). sections.content: The documentary's exploration of class barriers in racing connects to films like **Ferrari: Race to Immortality** (2017) and **McLaren** (2017), which show how money and connections increasingly dominated the sport from the 1970s onward. Byrne's story serves as a cautionary tale about talent being insufficient in a sport that requires millions in backing, similar to themes in **The Last Race** (2018), which examines the decline of working-class racing culture.
